It demonstrates that pre-commitment not only initiates but also drives opportunity creation, which in turn enhances international performance. Moreover, affordable loss and staging logic fully mediate this rela- tionship by mitigating uncertainties and facilitating incremental market adaptation. Experiential learning further moderates the relationship, as more experienced SMEs leverage accumulated knowledge for enhanced performance. Considering effectual thinking along with real options reasoning, this study provides empirical evidence that SMEs can strategically navigate uncertainty through incremental, resource- constrained investments. A post hoc analysis reveals that internationalized SMEs employ early stakeholder agreements, affordable loss caps, and pilot initiatives to create more market entry opportunities. All in all, our findings offer a structured framework for SME managers, emphasizing flexible, adaptive decision-making and experiential learning to achieve sustainable international expansion, validated using survey data and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) analysis. Traditional internationalization theories, such as transaction cost economies (TCE) and the Uppsala Model, emphasize predictive strategies, assuming firms can carefully plan expansions when adequate information is available (Ahi et al., 2019). For many SMEs, however, these predictive approaches are risky and impractical because of limited resources and liabilities like smallness. They may lock scarce resources into rigid commitments, leaving little room to adapt when market conditions shift (Smolka et al., 2018). Effectuation theory offers an alternative and entrepreneurial lens, promoting flexibility and experimentation in resource-constrained settings (Sarasvathy, 2001; Sarasvathy & Dew, 2008a, b). Rather than following a fixed plan, effectual decision- makers focus on the means at hand, such as networks, knowledge, and finances, and set manageable limits on investments, known as “affordable loss,” to reduce down- side risk (Calabrese et al., 2017; Caputo et al., 2018). Additionally, early stakeholder engagement, or pre-commitment, helps reduce uncertainty by securing external sup- port before major investments (Dew et al., 2009; Zaki et al., 2015). This emphasis on real-time learning is crucial for SMEs operating in dynamic, uncertain international markets. On the other hand, real options reasoning (ROR) provides a predictive-oriented framework for managing uncertainty (Townsend et al., 2018; Trigeorgis, 1996). ROR views international expansion as a sequence of smaller, staged investment decisions. At each stage, SMEs evaluate market feedback and choose whether to proceed, pause, or pivot (Chi et al., 2019; McGrath, 1999). In this vein, effectuation’s experimental mindset aligns closely with ROR’s staging logic, allowing SMEs to stay nimble and scale their commitment based on evolving information. Despite increasing interest in how SMEs internationalize under uncertainty, lim- ited empirical research has considered effectuation and ROR into a unified frame- work (Ahi et al., 2017; Casson & Gulamhussen, 2004; Hunt et al., 2021). Prior studies often studied these logics separately, focusing either on entrepreneurial reasoning or flexible investment strategy. This study addresses that gap by examin- ing how pre-commitment, affordable loss, and staging logic work together to foster foreign market entry (FME) opportunity creation. We also explore the moderating role of experiential learning, which is a common mechanism in both approaches, specifically, whether international experience strengthens the link between created opportunities and international performance (Calabrese et al., 2017; Caputo et al., 2022; Reymen et al., 2015). To guide this investigation, we ask two core questions: 1. How do effectual and real options components (pre-commitment, staging logic, and affordable loss) influence FME opportunity creation? 2. What role does experiential learning play in strengthening the link between FME opportunity creation and international performance? 1 3 International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal… Page 3 of 27 8 To investigate these questions, we conducted a survey of 332 New Zealand SMEs and analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), supplemented by qualitative responses. By answering these questions, we make three key contributions. First, it advances effectuation theory by clarify- ing how risk-limiting (affordable loss) and risk-sharing (pre-commitment) strategies align with the incremental logic of real options. Second, it shows that experiential learning acts as a catalyst, helping firms refine strategies through feedback and mar- ket encounters. Third, it provides practical insights for SME managers, demonstrating how phased commitments, early stakeholder agreements, and “affordable-to-lose” investments can collectively reduce market entry risks. All in all, this study proposes an integrated framework that demonstrates the value of combining effectuation and ROR to support SME internationalization. By empiri- cally testing how these logics intersect, we offer new insights into decision-making under uncertainty, particularly for resource-constrained SMEs entering highly uncer- tain international markets. Theoretical background Entering foreign markets can be a daunting prospect for SMEs. They typically have fewer resources than larger firms, making them more vulnerable to unpredictable foreign markets (Ahi et al., 2019). To address this uncertainty, researchers have explored two complementary decision-making logics: effectuation (a control-ori- ented approach) and real options reasoning (a predictive-oriented approach), empha- sizing flexibility and incremental approaches to risk. Effectuation and SMEs’ international performance Effectuation theory offers a flexible framework for understanding how SMEs can thrive in international markets with limited resources and high uncertainty (Mauer et al., 2021; Sarasvathy, 2001). Rather than following rigid predictions or rigid strate- gies, effectuation encourages entrepreneurs to leverage what they already have, such as personal networks, specialized knowledge, and financial resources, and then adapt as conditions change. This means-driven logic enables SMEs to respond rapidly and entrepreneurially to foreign market uncertainty (Dew et al., 2011; Wiltbank et al., 2009). Two of the most important aspects of effectuation are affordable loss and pre- commitment, which directly address how SMEs can manage and mitigate uncertainty and harness external support. Affordable loss involves establishing clear boundaries on the maximum resources, time, money, or other assets a firm is willing to commit at each step of its international expansion (Schweizer et al., 2010). By capping potential downsides, SMEs remain agile and flexible, able to experiment with new markets without jeopardizing the entire business if an initiative fails. Meanwhile, pre-commitment centers on forging early agreements with key stakeholders, whether suppliers, distributors, or pilot customers, to share risks and resources (Smolka et al., 2018; Laari-Salmela et al., 2021). By partnering with local 1 3 8 Page 4 of 27International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal (2026) 22:8 players in destination markets before making significant investments, SMEs gain crucial insights into consumer preferences, regulatory requirements, and competi- tive conditions. This approach reduces uncertainty and fosters mutual trust since stakeholders have a vested interest in the venture’s success. Together, affordable loss and pre-commitment enable an iterative, risk-managed internationalization process where SMEs learn and adjust through real-time experimentation (McGrath & Mac- Millan, 2000). Effectuation, therefore, provides SMEs with a practical and entrepre- neurial path to decision-making grounded in ongoing learning and flexibility. This approach is especially relevant in international markets, where sudden shifts in con- sumer demand, currency fluctuations, or competitive pressures can render long-term predictions unreliable (Mainela et al., 2014). By emphasizing resource-conscious action and shared risk-taking, effectual reasoning helps SMEs stay ambitious and cautious in uncertain global markets. Real options reasoning (ROR) and incremental approach to internationalization SMEs often face significant uncertainties when expanding to foreign markets. At the same time, ROR breaks down expansion into smaller steps, or “options,” that can be tested at each stage (Ahi et al., 2017; Trigeorgis & Lambertides, 2014). For example, SMEs might begin by launching a small pilot or forming a joint venture, then proceed, pivot, or pause based on market feedback (Kogut & Kulatilaka, 2001; Dixit et al., 1994). By considering staging logic, ROR fits well with the affordable loss principle. SMEs can manage potential failures by calculating how much they invest in each phase. Moreover, staging logic reinforces pre-commitment by enabling firms to involve partners in phased, lower-risk engagements (Chi & Huang, 2023; McGrath, 1999). Being able to stop, exit, or change quickly is especially helpful in highly uncertain environments, where rapid shifts can lead to steep losses if a firm is overly committed (Townsend et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2021). By doing so, as SMEs gain experience in each new market, they develop a deeper knowledge of cultural dif- ferences, competition, and customer needs (Alinasab et al., 2022; Chin et al., 2022; Vahlne & Johanson, 2017). This iterative and experiential learning process may enhance international performance over time because firms become more adept at spotting opportunities and managing risk. These insights echo the Uppsala model, which describes how firms learn incre- mentally from each foreign venture to reduce uncertainty (Johanson & Vahlne, 2009). Similarly, the resource-based view (RBV) (Barney, 1991) highlights how unique organizational resources and capabilities, such as specialized knowledge gained through learning, can form the basis for competitive advantage in foreign markets. Considering behavioral components of effectuation along with ROR provides SMEs with an adaptive, flexible, risk-aware strategy for foreign market entries. Effectuation keeps them flexible and reliant on the resources they already have, while ROR adds a structured method of testing market possibilities step by step (Ahi et al., 2019; Chi & Huang, 2023; Hunt et al., 2021). Each market entry generates new insights that feed back into future decisions, helping managers refine their strategies for achieving better international performance. These perspectives allow SMEs to 1 3 International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal… Page 5 of 27 8 engage in low-commitment incrementally and high-learning international strategies that improve long-term performance while managing short-term uncertainty. Conceptual framework and hypotheses development Pre-commitment and FME opportunity creation Pre-commitment is an SME’s effort to secure stakeholder support and resources early in internationalization, thereby reducing uncertainty before major investments (Caputo et al., 2023; Vanderstraeten et al., 2020). For example, partnering with a local research firm can yield valuable market insights at a low cost (Cui et al., 2023; Del Giudice et al., 2017). Such early agreements foster trust and legitimacy, enabling SMEs to identify market gaps, understand local needs, and develop effective offer- ings (Alinasab et al., 2022; Etemad, 2023). Thus, pre-commitment may directly enhance FME opportunity creation by equipping SMEs with a solid knowledge base and resources for new market entry. Hypothesis 1 (H1): Pre-commitment positively influences FME opportunity creation by enabling SMEs to leverage stakeholder resources to experiment, learn, and adapt. Affordable loss, staging logic, and the mediation effect Although pre-commitment can drive opportunity creation, it is often insufficient for long-term success in unpredictable markets, as SMEs must also manage risks and remain flexible. Affordable loss limits SMEs’ resources at each stage, ensuring finan- cial stability even if a venture fails (Dew et al., 2009; Hunt et al., 2021; Martina, 2020). Staging logic segments the internationalization process into smaller, manage- able phases, allowing firms to pause, pivot, or expand based on feedback (Caputo et al., 2023; Hult et al., 2010; Ipsmiller et al., 2019). Together, affordable loss and staging logic convert pre-commitments into actionable strategies, enabling SMEs to experiment in uncertain environments without overextending resources (Nicholls- Nixon et al., 2021). Consequently, the direct effect of pre-commitment may become non-significant when affordable loss and staging logic are applied, as these mecha- nisms fully drive opportunity creation. Hypothesis 2 (H2): Affordable loss and staging logic mediate the relationship between pre-commitment and FME opportunity creation by enabling SMEs to take measured risks and adapt dynamically. FME opportunity creation and international performance FME opportunity creation is critical for SMEs with limited resources striving for sustainable international performance. By proactively identifying and developing opportunities in foreign markets, SMEs build valuable connections with customers, 1 3 8 Page 6 of 27International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal (2026) 22:8 suppliers, and stakeholders, laying the groundwork for long-term success (Chetty et al., 2024). Opportunity creation also provides insights into market needs and competi- tive dynamics, enabling SMEs to build competitive advantages over time (Schweizer, 2012). Effectuation principles, including affordable loss and pre-commitment, bal- ance exploration, and risk management, support opportunity creation, while staging logic reinforces this process by enabling continuous assessment and adaptation (Buc- cieri et al., 2023; Caputo et al., 2020). Thus, SMEs that effectively create opportuni- ties are better positioned to expand market share, enhance profitability, and achieve sustainable growth. Hypothesis 3 (H3): FME opportunity creation positively influences international performance, as SMEs that effectively capitalize on foreign market opportunities achieve superior growth and profitability. Experiential learning as a moderator Experiential learning, which applies insights from past experiences to refine future actions, is a mechanism in SME internationalization. Through trial and adaptation (i.e., act and see logic), SMEs gain a deeper understanding of market dynamics, enabling more informed and effective decision-making (Alinasab, 2022; Gabrielsson & Gabrielsson, 2013). This learning-by-doing approach improves risk assessment, resource allocation, and opportunity creation (Camisón & Villar-López, 2010). As SMEs accumulate international experience, they become adept at managing cultural differences, regulatory frameworks, and market uncertainties (Chin et al., 2022; Corbett, 2005). Experiential learning may amplify the impact of FME opportunity creation on international performance by equipping SMEs with the knowledge and confidence needed for superior strategic decisions. Hypothesis 4 (H4): Experiential learning moderates the relationship between FME opportunity creation and international performance, strengthening the effect of opportunity creation as SMEs gain international experience. Affordable loss logic reflects the firm’s approach to limiting downside risk by aligning investments with acceptable thresholds. This construct was measured with five items adapted from Chandler et al. (2011) and Martin-Navarro et al. (2021). Measured using four items adapted from Chandler et al. (2011), this construct reflects a firm’s ability to leverage past knowledge to man- age and mitigate uncertainties. First, we accounted for firm-specific factors, as prior studies suggest that firm size (measured by the number of employees) and firm age (measured by years since estab- lishment) can influence the thoroughness of decision-making, with larger and older firms typically having more resources and experience (Haseeb et al., 2019; Kock, 2015). Analysis and results Analysis We employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the hypotheses, following Hair Jr et al. (2017) guidelines for robustness. PLS-SEM suits exploratory research and theoretical model development. We also conducted a complementary thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006; Ringle et al., 2023) for qualitative responses, providing richer practical insights. To test the hypothesized mediation effects and the direct relationships among pre-commitment, foreign market entry opportunity creation, and international per- formance, we followed Gaskin et al. (2023) recommended approach for testing medi- ation in structural models. We evaluated the significance of the parameter estimates using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples (Hair & Alamer, 2022; Hair et al. Jr, 2017). In this bootstrapping process, each resample had the same number of cases as the original dataset, allowing us to calculate reliable standard errors and assess the statis- tical significance of both direct and indirect effects (Hayes & Preacher, 2010; Ringle et al., 2023). This approach helped us thoroughly evaluate the mediating/moderating factors. Based on their theoretical relevance, we identified firm size and age as suitable instruments for pre-commitments. Firm size is linked to pre-commitments because larger firms typically have greater resources to handle internal uncertainties and com- mit to decisions incrementally. Similarly, firm age can influence pre-commitments as older firms are likely to possess more experience and structured processes, yet it does not directly affect constructs such as affordable loss or staging logic, confirm- ing its suitability as an instrument. In contrast, experience in international business was excluded as an instrument due to its direct impact on FME opportunity creation through enhanced market knowledge, thereby violating the exclusion restriction. The first-stage regression yielded a strong F-statistic (F = 16.15, p < 0.001), provid- ing empirical evidence of the strength of the instruments. Additionally, the Hansen J-test confirmed no over-identification issues (p > 0.05), supporting the validity of the selected instruments. Furthermore, we applied the control function approach, regressing endogenous variables on exogenous variables and instruments to obtain residuals, which were subsequently included in the structural model. Post hoc exploratory findings To complement the quantitative analyses, we conducted a post hoc exploratory inves- tigation to deepen our understanding of how SMEs operationalize pre-commitment, staging logic, and affordable loss in foreign market entry decisions. Additionally, we sought to explore the role of experiential learning in shaping these strategies under uncertain international contexts. Survey participants were invited to provide open-ended responses to two key questions: (1) the practical steps they took when initially entering a foreign market and (2) the lessons learned that influenced subse- quent entrepreneurial internationalization decisions. 124 substantive responses were received and thematically analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s (2006) framework. The findings revealed four primary themes, enriching and contextualizing the quantitative results. Contextualizing pre-commitment Approximately one-third of respondents emphasized the importance of early stake- holder engagement as a means of reducing uncertainty and facilitating market entry. 1 3 International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal… Page 19 of 27 8 These managers described pre-commitment as a contractual necessity and a rela- tional strategy to build trust and legitimacy. For example, a software CEO noted: Our early alliance with a local IT reseller de-risked our first overseas venture. Their willingness to pilot our product gave us immediate access to potential clients, letting us avoid big upfront investments. Such accounts underscore how pre-commitment mitigates knowledge gaps and accelerates knowledge transfer, aligning with the quantitative finding that pre-com- mitment fosters FME opportunity creation. Stakeholder involvement provided SMEs with critical resources and legitimacy, enabling smoother initial market traction. Refining staging logic through incremental learning About one-quarter of the responses provided detailed examples of staging logic in action, illustrating how SMEs adopt incremental approaches to foreign market entry. Many described launching small-scale operations, pilot tests, or limited product batches to gather market feedback and guide subsequent investments. A manufactur- ing sector participant explained: We viewed our first-year export plan as a ‘paid learning experience.’ Each phase, initial testing, small product batches, scaling up, was contingent on prior outcomes. These stepwise strategies reflect ROR, allowing SMEs to preserve flexibility while adapting to evolving market conditions. The ability to exercise or abandon “options” based on feedback highlights staging logic as a critical mediator that transforms pre- commitments into actionable FME opportunities. Operationalizing affordable loss Affordable loss emerged as a key strategy for mitigating risk, with approximately 30% of respondents explicitly describing efforts to set financial or resource thresh- olds. This approach allowed SMEs to manage uncertainty by capping potential losses and pacing investments. A food-and-beverage sector respondent shared: We defined the maximum we would invest in initial foreign marketing. Once we reached that cap, we assessed results before pouring in more funds. These practices illustrate how affordable loss provides a practical mechanism for lim- iting overinvestment in unfamiliar markets. Several respondents combined affordable loss with staging logic, implementing subsequent phases only after achieving pre- defined performance thresholds. This interplay reinforces the importance of afford- able loss and staging logic as complementary mediators in FME opportunity creation. 1 3 8 Page 20 of 27International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal (2026) 22:8 Role of experiential learning Experiential learning emerged as a unifying thread across the responses, highlight- ing its influence on decision-making and strategy refinement. Approximately 15% of participants explicitly linked their internationalization experiences to improved market interpretation, partnership formation, and risk management. A consulting firm manager observed: Our earlier ventures in Australia taught us how to structure risk-sharing deals. We replicated that approach in Southeast Asia but adapted the payment mile- stones to fit cultural norms. These insights demonstrate how experiential learning moderates the relationship between FME opportunity creation and international performance. Repeated expo- sure to international contexts equips SMEs with the knowledge to refine their use of pre-commitment, affordable loss, and staging logic, enhancing their ability to adapt to diverse foreign markets. Discussion Our findings demonstrate that pre-commitment, or securing stakeholder support and resources early, significantly drives SMEs’ foreign market entry opportunities. While pre-commitment alone reduces uncertainty and fosters initial trust, integrating it with affordable loss and staging logic provides SMEs with a more structured and robust approach to internationalization. Affordable loss limits investment uncertainties at each stage while staging logic allows incremental progress based on real-time market feedback, preventing SMEs from excessive resource exposure. These insights align with previous studies emphasizing adaptive strategies under uncertainty. For example, Buccieri et al. (2023) and Smolka et al. (2018) similarly show that iterative, resource-conscious approaches enhance performance in unfa- miliar markets. Their findings resonate with our conclusion that SMEs benefit sub- stantially from effectual thinking combined with careful uncertainty management, enabling iterative learning and flexibility without large-scale financial risks. This per- spective supports the view that smaller experimental investments foster innovation and strategic flexibility (Ahi et al., 2017). However, our findings diverge from research advocating extensive structured planning for rapid international growth. Chetty et al. (2024) and Morais and Ferreira (2020) suggest that detailed planning can expedite market penetration, especially for resource-rich firms. Our study suggests flexible and staged approaches are typically more viable and sustainable for resource-constrained SMEs. Instead of committing significant resources upfront, SMEs in our sample relied heavily on real-time feed- back to dynamically adjust their strategies, a tactic particularly suitable for uncertain markets. Experiential learning further enhances SMEs’ flexibility capabilities. Firms ini- tially expanding into culturally similar markets (e.g., from New Zealand to Australia) 1 3 International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal… Page 21 of 27 8 gain critical insights for refining their strategies before entering more distant or chal- lenging markets. This incremental learning aligns with the Uppsala model (Johanson & Vahlne, 2009), highlighting how each foreign venture enriches SMEs’ strategic knowledge and improves their effectiveness in future internationalization efforts. Post hoc qualitative insights Qualitative findings reinforce how SMEs operationalize pre-commitment, affordable loss, and staging logic in real-world practice. Respondents emphasized pre-commit- ment’s role in reducing uncertainty and achieving market traction through partner- ships, such as collaborations with local resellers or distributors, to quickly validate market potential. These practical insights illustrate that pre-commitments effectively legitimize SMEs’ market entry efforts and establish early trust. Respondents also highlighted staging logic’s value, highlighting how incremen- tal, reversible steps enable strategic testing without significant risk exposure. They described their initial export strategy as a “paid learning experience,” demonstrating how SMEs use staging logic to manage market uncertainty effectively. Such real- world examples confirm staging logic’s mediating role between pre-commitment and opportunity creation as SMEs adapt strategies based on market feedback. The affordable loss principle emerged clearly, with managers deliberately limiting initial investments to manage uncertainty. Participants commonly described allocat- ing fixed budgets for initial marketing or product trials and advancing further only after meeting established performance thresholds. These practices illustrate effectual reasoning in action, demonstrating the utility of affordable loss in minimizing finan- cial risks while pursuing international opportunities. Experiential learning consistently appeared as a critical moderating factor, enhanc- ing SMEs’ capabilities in foreign markets. Managers highlighted how previous inter- nationalization experiences improved their ability to structure pre-commitments, set realistic affordable loss limits, and strategically stage investments. This iterative learning process aligns with effectuation literature emphasizing flexibility (Prashan- tham et al., 2019; Sarasvathy, 2024) and further validates the Uppsala model, illus- trating experiential learning’s pivotal role in SMEs’ international performance. Contributions and managerial implications This study advances effectuation theory and international entrepreneurship literature by integrating affordable loss and staging logic into conceptualizing FME oppor- tunity creation. Our findings offer SMEs a structured yet flexible decision-making framework suitable for resource-constrained, uncertain markets by synthesizing ROR with effectual logic. Unlike studies emphasizing purely predictive or entirely control-oriented flexible strategies, we show how SMEs can use affordable loss and staging logic together to balance commitment and flexibility effectively (Schweizer, 2012). This synergic approach reinforces the resource-based view (RBV), highlight- 1 3 8 Page 22 of 27International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal (2026) 22:8 ing resource-conscious strategies as vital for SMEs’ sustainable growth in interna- tional markets (Barney, 1991; Caputo et al., 2021; Wernerfelt, 2013). A key theoretical contribution is identifying experiential learning as an impor- tant moderator that enhances the relationship between FME opportunity creation and international performance. By demonstrating that SMEs continuously refine their strategies through international experiences, this study bridges effectuation theory and experiential learning models (i.e., the Uppsala Model), highlighting how ongoing learning shapes SMEs’ international effectiveness. From a practical standpoint, SME managers should prioritize securing early stake- holder agreements (pre-commitments), adopting staged investments based on market feedback (staging logic), and carefully managing financial exposure through afford- able loss thresholds. Additionally, managers should systematically capture lessons from each market entry to strengthen future internationalization strategies, leverag- ing experiential learning as a source of sustained competitive advantage. Our find- ings equip SMEs with clear guidelines for managing and mitigating uncertainty in international markets, fostering strategic growth despite resource limitations. Future research directions and limitations Despite offering valuable insights into how SMEs manage uncertainty in foreign markets, this study has some limitations. First, the reliance on self-reported data may introduce response bias, with managers potentially overstating or understating their use of strategies such as affordable loss or staging logic. Future research could miti- gate this issue by collecting third-party data, such as supplier or customer feedback, or by conducting qualitative studies to validate survey responses. Second, although our sample includes seven diverse industries, generalizability to sectors with significantly different operational risks or investment demands remains limited. Industries such as pharmaceuticals or financial services, with distinct risk profiles and regulatory complexities, were not represented. Expanding future studies to cover a broader range of sectors could reveal important differences in how SMEs apply effectual and real options reasoning. Third, while our sample size meets standard guidelines for Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), a larger sample (e.g., 416 participants based on gamma exponential approach recommended by Kock & Hadaya, 2018) could further enhance statistical power and the reliability of findings. Collaborating with industry bodies or international networks might help achieve this larger scope. Additionally, our study adopted a cross-sectional rather than longitudinal approach, limiting insights into how adaptive strategies evolve as SMEs accumulate interna- tional experience or encounter changing market conditions. Longitudinal research could better capture the dynamic nature of entrepreneurial internationalization, high- lighting how strategies such as affordable loss and staging logic change over time. Finally, future research could explore how emerging digital tools such as AI and real-time data analytics influence SMEs’ effectuation and real options decision-mak- ing. Investigating how digitalization facilitates strategic pivots, collaborative partner- 1 3 International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal… Page 23 of 27 8 ships, or improved risk assessment would significantly extend current knowledge on SME internationalization. Conclusion This study provides a strategic framework that helps SMEs better manage uncertainty during entrepreneurial internationalization. Our findings demonstrate that combining pre-commitment, affordable loss, and staging logic allows SMEs to balance risk and flexibility, enhancing foreign market entry opportunities and international perfor- mance. Additionally, experiential learning is an important moderating factor, further refining SMEs’ adaptive strategies. While limited by self-reported data, a cross- sectional design, and industry-specific sampling, this research advances our under- standing of SMEs’ strategic responses to uncertainty. Future research should adopt longitudinal methods, broaden industry contexts, and explore the role of digital tech- nologies. Overall, this study offers practical insights enabling SMEs to achieve sus- tainable growth through resource-conscious, iterative internationalization strategies. JSON: Name: precommitment_affordableloss_staging_sme Title: PLS-SEM investigation of how pre-commitment, affordable loss, and staging logic affect foreign market entry opportunity creation and international performance in SMEs Short Hypothesis: In SMEs, pre-commitment increases foreign market entry opportunity creation through the mediating effects of affordable loss and staging logic, which in turn raises international performance. Related Work: Prior work divides into two streams: effectuation-based decision theories (emphasizing means-driven reasoning, affordable loss limits, and early stakeholder pre-commitments) and real-options or incremental approaches (emphasizing staged investments and option-like sequential decision-making). Effectuation studies have shown how resource-constrained firms use affordable loss and stakeholder commitments to reduce downside risk, but many are qualitative, small-sample, or examine individual components in isolation. Real-options research provides formal mechanisms for staging and option valuation but rarely incorporates behavioral, stakeholder-oriented mechanisms like pre-commitment or affordable loss. Existing empirical studies often treat causation and effectuation as competing logics rather than interacting mechanisms, lack integrated mediation/moderation tests, and are frequently cross-sectional with limited generalizability across industries and small-open economies. Measurement and method weaknesses include limited use of robust mediation/moderation testing, potential common-method bias, and underuse of combined quantitative–qualitative validation. Abstract: This research addresses how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can translate early stakeholder pre-commitments into sustained international performance under uncertainty. We propose an integrated empirical framework that combines behavioral effectuation principles (pre-commitment and affordable loss) with real-options reasoning (staging logic) and tests experiential learning as a moderator. The approach uses quantitative structural modeling of decision mechanisms and opportunity creation, complemented by qualitative thematic analysis of practitioner accounts. The primary contribution is an empirically validated causal pathway showing that pre-commitments drive opportunity creation primarily via affordable loss and staged investment logic, and that accumulated experiential learning amplifies the conversion of opportunities into performance. The expected outcome is a validated, testable framework that identifies specific managerial decision levers—early stakeholder agreements, capped loss thresholds, and incremental pilots—that SMEs can use to balance risk and adaptability during international expansion. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary cross-sectional survey of SMEs active in international markets (target N≥300) with multi-item measures for pre-commitment, affordable loss, staging logic, FME opportunity creation, experiential learning, and international performance; (2) Replication datasets: independent SME surveys from at least two other small-open economies and firm-level export/performance administrative data where available; (3) Qualitative dataset: open-ended responses from survey respondents (N≥100) for thematic validation. Baselines: (A) Effectuation-only structural model (pre-commitment and affordable loss → FME creation → performance); (B) ROR-only model (staging logic → FME creation → performance); (C) Causal/predictive-only model (predictive antecedents → FME creation) ; (D) Null model with controls only. Methods and setup: estimate structural relationships using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) to obtain path coefficient significance; report R2, SRMR, Q2 predict, f2 effect sizes, and confidence intervals for indirect effects; test mediation using product-of-coefficients and bootstrapped indirect effects; test moderation by adding interaction term (FME creation × experiential learning) and probe simple slopes at ±1 SD; robustness checks: (i) Gaussian copula endogeneity tests, (ii) instrumental variable two-stage approach using firm size and firm age as instruments, (iii) covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) for comparative fit, (iv) multi-group analyses by industry and by international experience tertiles, (v) common-method bias checks including marker variable and full collinearity VIFs. Ablation studies: remove one mediator at a time (affordable loss or staging logic) and compare change in indirect effect sizes; remove moderator to quantify attenuation of the FME→performance link. Baseline comparisons: compare explained variance and predictive power across baselines (A–D) and the integrated model. Evaluation metrics: statistical significance (p<0.05), standardized path coefficients, change in R2, indirect effect size and significance, SRMR<0.08, Q2>0 for predictive relevance, Cohen’s f2 for local effect sizes; qualitative validation: thematic coding frequency and co-occurrence mapping for evidence of mechanisms. Pre-registration: pre-register hypotheses, measurement model, and analysis plan; perform sensitivity analyses for sample size assumptions. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report and common-method bias in survey measures may inflate associations between constructs; cross-sectional design limits strong causal inference and temporal sequencing of mediation; instruments (firm size, age) may not fully satisfy exclusion restrictions and residual endogeneity may remain; sample representativeness risks if SMEs come from a single country or narrow industry mix, limiting generalization to larger firms or high-capital sectors; measurement validity risk from adapting multi-item scales across cultural contexts; complex SEM with multiple mediators and moderator requires substantial sample size—underpowered tests may yield false negatives for moderation or multi-group analyses; qualitative data may be sparse or non-representative, limiting thematic triangulation; replication datasets may differ in regulatory or market structure, complicating cross-country comparisons; computational overhead for bootstrapped SEM and robustness checks rises with larger replication panels, constraining rapid iteration.
